title: Space Station Crew Returns Home; New Astronauts Begin 6‑Month Mission – CBS News
body:
The International Space Station will welcome a fresh crew this week as the current expedition departs, marking the end of an eight‑month stay for four veterans and the start of a six‑month rotation of astronauts from the United States, Europe and Russia. The departing team – NASA astronauts Frank Rubio and Stephen Bowen, European Space Agency astronaut Matthias Maurer and Roscosmos cosmonaut Anton Shkaplerov – boarded SpaceX’s Crew Dragon Endeavour on Wednesday, undocked from the orbital laboratory and began the fiery descent that will culminate in a splash‑down in the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of southern Florida on Thursday.

The hand‑over is the latest in a series of crew exchanges that keep the ISS continuously inhabited, a practice that began in 2000 and has become a logistical choreography involving multiple space agencies and commercial partners. The outgoing crew’s mission was notable for several scientific firsts, including the longest continuous U.S. spacewalk in more than a decade and a series of experiments on protein crystal growth that could inform future drug development. Their tenure also saw the station’s power‑generation capacity increase after the installation of new solar arrays, boosting the platform’s ability to support more ambitious research payloads.

The incoming quartet – NASA’s veteran commander Loral O’Malley, ESA astronaut Samantha Crisp, JAXA’s Koichi Watanabe and Roscosmos cosmonaut Dmitry Petrov – will assume command of the station for a six‑month stint. Their agenda reflects a shift toward deeper exploration and commercial utilization. Among the priorities are the testing of the European “Axiom” habitat module, slated to dock later this year, and the continuation of the NASA‑led “Gateway” program’s experiments that simulate lunar surface conditions. In addition, the crew will oversee the first commercial cargo resupply mission operated by a private Japanese firm, a milestone that underscores the growing role of non‑governmental actors in low‑Earth orbit.

The transition also carries geopolitical significance. While the United States and its commercial partners have taken a leading role in crew transportation since the retirement of the Russian Soyuz in 2020, Russia’s continued presence on the ISS demonstrates a pragmatic collaboration that persists despite broader tensions on Earth. The joint operation of Crew Dragon and the Russian “Nauka” module illustrates how scientific goals can bridge diplomatic divides, a pattern that may inform future multinational endeavors such as the Lunar Gateway and eventual crewed missions to Mars.

From an operational standpoint, the splash‑down will be monitored by recovery vessels stationed near the Atlantic recovery zone, with NASA’s recovery team prepared to retrieve the crew and the capsule’s scientific payloads. The mission’s success hinges on precise re‑entry calculations, heat‑shield integrity and flawless parachute deployment—systems that have proven reliable across more than a dozen Crew Dragon flights. Once aboard the recovery ship, the astronauts will undergo a series of medical examinations and de‑briefings before returning to Johnson Space Center for a period of rest and training.

Looking ahead, the new crew’s arrival sets the stage for a bustling period of research, technology demonstration and international cooperation aboard the ISS. With commercial entities increasingly delivering cargo and crew, and with plans to extend the station’s operational life through at least 2030, the seamless hand‑over underscores a maturing low‑Earth orbit ecosystem. As humanity prepares for deeper voyages to the Moon and beyond, the ISS continues to serve as both a proving ground and a diplomatic bridge, proving that sustained collaboration in space remains both possible and essential.
